key_insight: Large language models can learn to suggest exact molecular edits that make synthetic routes more feasible, rather than just generating new molecules. This helps preserve useful chemical features while improving synthesizability and outperforming traditional optimization methods.
problem_solved: Many molecules produced by computational drug design are difficult or impossible to synthesize in practice. The paper tackles the challenge of predicting precise structural edits that convert these molecules into more synthesizable ones without losing important properties.
method: Use a large language model to predict a sequence of structural edits for a target molecule.
Frame synthesizability optimization as an edit-sequence prediction problem instead of full de novo molecule generation.
Guide the model to make targeted changes that preserve key molecular features while improving synthetic feasibility.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners in chemistry and drug discovery, this shows a practical way to move from generative design to actionable molecule refinement. It can improve the usability of AI-designed compounds by making them more realistic for downstream synthesis and experimentation.
visual_elements: Before-and-after molecule diagram showing an unsynthesizable molecule transformed into a synthesizable one
Flowchart of the pipeline: input molecule -> LLM-predicted edit sequence -> optimized molecule
Comparison chart of performance versus traditional synthesizability optimization methods
Highlighted structural edits on molecular sketches to show preserved vs modified regions
paper_title: Guiding large language models to predict edit sequences for molecular synthesizability optimization
